findings.paper_title: MTFP - Scene Setting - General Fund report and Appendices 1-5
findings.headline: MTFP assumes maximum allowable Council Tax increases without referendum (2.99% annually) projected to generate £1.995 million cumulative additional income by 2030/31
findings.detail: Council plans to maximize government's allowable Council Tax increase threshold without triggering referendum, assumed at 2.99% annually throughout the MTFP period. This strategy is expected to generate annual additional income of £473.5k in 2027/28 rising to £524.6k by 2030/31, totaling £1.995m cumulative additional income. Council is explicitly adopting this as part of strategy to 'make the most of the local tax raising flexibilities as set out by Central Government'.
findings.matters: Shows council maximizing available tax levers; continued reliance on government maintaining 2.99% referendum threshold; cumulative £2m of identified income contributes meaningfully to bridging the deficit; pattern demonstrates all councils pushing local tax hard due to government funding shortfall.
findings.quote: The MTFP assumes the Council will increase Band D Council Tax to the maximum level permitted without triggering a referendum. These increases over the period have the potential to generate an additional annual income of £1.995 million by 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: MTFP - Scene Setting - General Fund report and Appendices 1-5
findings.headline: Fees and charges strategy has delivered £2.5 million additional income over three years, exceeding 20% target; car parking and Keyhaven charges increased from 1 January 2027
findings.detail: Council achieved approximately £2.5m additional fees and charges income over 2024/25–2026/27, surpassing the 20% growth target (equivalent to 6.3% annualised). From 1 January 2027, car parking fees increased generating estimated £189k additional annual income; Keyhaven river fees increased generating £7k. For 2027/28 onwards, policy shifts to use CPI as guideline for annual uplifts unless alternative approach justified by market conditions.
findings.matters: Demonstrates fees and charges as reliable and effective income lever; shows council has successfully extracted growth and has potential for further increases; provides benchmark for peer councils on achievable growth rates; is part of strategy to offset structural deficit.
findings.figures: £2.5m additional income over 3 years (2024/25–2026/27); car parking additional income £189k from 1 January 2027; Keyhaven additional income £7k from 1 January 2027; fees and charges growth target £300k for 2027/28
findings.quote: During this three year period the Council generated approximately £2.5 million of additional gross fees and charges income, thereby surpassing its 20% target.

findings.paper_title: MTFP - Scene Setting - General Fund report and Appendices 1-5
findings.headline: Waste service budget impacts still being resolved with resource adjustments pending completion of review of new service model
findings.detail: New waste service has been fully rolled out district-wide following significant one-off investment (temporary staff, bin acquisition, delivery, advisory support). A full operational review is now underway. Report states that 'full clarity on the budget requirements for future years is still being established and resources may need to be adjusted once the review has concluded and the new ways of working are fully defined'.
findings.matters: Creates contingent adjustment risk to MTFP forecasts; budget assumptions will change once review concludes; illustrates timing lag between service transformation and financial stabilization; review could reveal operational pressures requiring additional investment or conversely identify efficiencies.
findings.figures: No quantum specified for future adjustments; current budget impact of £54k reduction in 2027/28 (net of various one-off items)
findings.quote: A full review of the new waste service is being conducted now that a consistent district wide service is being provided. Any adjustments to budgets will need to be included in future updates.

findings.paper_title: MTFP - Scene Setting - General Fund report and Appendices 1-5
findings.headline: Investment income budget cut by £250,000 in each of 2027/28 and 2028/29 as interest rates fall and cash drawdown increases
findings.detail: Council reduced investment income budget by £250k for both 2027/28 and 2028/29 despite achieving investment income better than budget in recent years. Reduction reflects acknowledgment of 'downward trend' in interest rates and 'increased requirement to utilise cash balances'. Bank of England base rate has fallen from 5.25% peak in 2023/24 to 3.75% currently.
findings.matters: Interest rate advantage councils briefly enjoyed is reversing; treasury income will continue to decline; removes a small source of positive variance that has helped balance budgets in recent years; forecasts higher cash burn rate.
findings.figures: Investment income reduction £250k in each of 2027/28 and 2028/29; base rate 3.75% (down from 5.25% peak)
findings.quote: in recognition of the downward trend and the increased requirement to utilise cash balances, the investment income budget has been reduced by £250,000 in both 2027/28 and 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: MTFP - Scene Setting - General Fund report and Appendices 1-5
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation additional resource requirements continuing to be quantified with £1.850 million reserve held but sufficiency uncertain
findings.detail: Following the recent pause to the LGR programme, the council is seeking cost recovery for amounts already spent on transition planning. However, 'additional resources are still likely to be required to support a safe and legally compliant transition'. Work is ongoing to quantify the required capacity across all council functions and determine whether existing budget provision and the £1.850m LGR reserve will be sufficient. Creates material uncertainty over future costs and reserve adequacy.
findings.matters: Material going concern uncertainty; LGR timeline is unconfirmed; additional transition costs may emerge; reserve of £1.850m may prove insufficient; affects medium-term financial sustainability and planning assumptions.
findings.figures: Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation Reserve £1.850m
findings.quote: Work is continuing to quantify the level of additional capacity required across all Council functions and to determine whether the existing budget provision and Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation Reserve are sufficient to meet these requirements.

findings.paper_title: MTFP - Scene Setting - General Fund report and Appendices 1-5
findings.headline: Equal pay claims proceeding to tribunal with unquantified potential financial settlement creating contingent liability
findings.detail: Council has received a small number of equal pay claims relating to historic working practices, due to proceed to tribunal. The council has not accepted the validity of any claims and is taking legal advice. The report includes potential settlement as a contingent liability in MTFP context but proceedings are not far enough advanced to quantify financial exposure. This represents a material unknown financial risk not captured in headline budget numbers.
findings.matters: Unquantified contingent liability not reflected in current forecasts; if claims succeed, could require significant budget amendment or reserve drawdown; illustrates historic employment/HR risk that could crystallize; timing and cost unknown.
findings.figures: Number of claims and quantum not specified
findings.quote: The potential for financial settlement warrants inclusion within the Medium Term Financial planning context for the Council, albeit proceedings are not far enough advanced to inform any specific assumptions at this stage.

findings.paper_title: MTFP - Scene Setting - General Fund report and Appendices 1-5
findings.headline: Budget Equalisation Reserve of £1.199 million explicitly identified as insufficient to mitigate scale of forecast budget gap
findings.detail: The council holds a £1.199m Budget Equalisation Reserve established to protect against unforeseen pressures and support the statutory obligation to deliver balanced budget. The report explicitly states this reserve 'is insufficient to mitigate the current scale of the budget gap' and emphasizes it can 'only be used once' and should 'only be regarded as a very short-term solution', limiting financial flexibility to absorb additional pressures.
findings.matters: Indicates the council cannot rely on reserves-based smoothing to manage the deficit; reserve will likely deplete rapidly; council has limited buffer for unexpected costs or income shortfalls; restricts ability to manage volatility in volatile income streams (e.g. EPR).
findings.figures: Budget Equalisation Reserve £1.199m against cumulative deficit £3.484m (reserve covers 34% of 4-year gap)
findings.quote: Furthermore, the reserve is insufficient to mitigate the current scale of the budget gap.

findings.paper_title: MTFP - Scene Setting - General Fund report and Appendices 1-5
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility waste income conservatively assumed to reduce 4% annually but faces risk of 20% taper reducing income by up to £500,000
findings.detail: The new EPR scheme is still bedding in with 'potential for variation'. The council has prudently included £100k annual reduction (4% taper) in future receipts. However, the report explicitly flags that 'a more significant reduction could well be seen, with an overall 20% taper equating to a total reduction of more like £500,000'. Current 2026/27 income budgeted at c£2.5m. Prior year (2025/26) required a government top-up after shortfall (stated as one-off and not to be repeated).
findings.matters: Material unquantified downside risk on a significant income stream; EPR scheme is new and volatile; if full 20% reduction occurs it represents more than half the 2027/28 deficit; directly affects waste cost recovery and may trigger further savings requirements.
findings.figures: Conservative assumption £100k annual taper (4%); potential downside £500k (20% taper); current income c£2.5m for 2026/27
findings.quote: there remains potential for variation, consequently the Council has prudently included an annual £100,000 tapering of future receipts (equivalent to a 4% reduction). A more significant reduction could well be seen, with an overall 20% taper equating to a total reduction of more like £500,000.

findings.paper_title: MTFP - Scene Setting - General Fund report and Appendices 1-5
findings.headline: Core spending power frozen over three-year settlement with government-determined resources declining from £9.974m to £9.780m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The 2026/27–2028/29 multi-year settlement left the council's core spending power effectively frozen. Government Determined Resources are: 2027/28 £9.974m, 2028/29 £9.495m, 2029/30 £9.694m, 2030/31 £9.780m. Council tax growth will now only offset government funding reductions rather than fund service growth or cost pressures.
findings.matters: Structural constraint on funding that affects all councils; shows government is not providing growth capacity to meet service demand inflation or pay/price pressures; forces councils to rely entirely on local taxation and income generation.
findings.quote: the Council's core spending power effectively frozen over the settlement period. This means that growth in Council Tax typically used to help support increases in costs will now instead only largely offset reductions in government support.

findings.paper_title: MTFP - Scene Setting - General Fund report and Appendices 1-5
findings.headline: General Fund deficit of £1.250 million in 2027/28 rising to £3.484 million cumulative by 2030/31
findings.detail: The council faces escalating annual deficits: £1.25m in 2027/28 (representing 5% of the £26.63m budget), growing to cumulative £2.443m by 2028/29 (9% of budget), and reaching cumulative £3.484m by 2030/31. The report states this scale of shortfall must be tackled through sustainable savings and income growth to meet the statutory obligation to set a fully balanced budget.
findings.matters: Scale and trajectory of deficit shows the council under significant structural pressure; peers track how others are managing similar gaps; lenders need to understand sustainability of the funding position.
findings.figures: 2027/28 deficit £1.250m (5% of budget); 2028/29 cumulative £2.443m (9% of budget); 2030/31 cumulative £3.484m
findings.quote: the forecast deficit to 2030/31 of £3.484 million is of absolute relevance to the financial planning of New Forest District Council.

findings.headline: Council is combining service reductions with senior manager sharing, job vacancy controls, process reviews, and planned Council Tax and fee increases
findings.detail: Beyond the consultation proposals, the council states it is already implementing efficiency measures including sharing senior managers with neighbouring councils, tighter controls on filling vacant positions, and reviewing internal processes. Separately, councillors will consider Council Tax increases 'permitted by Government' and increases to fees and charges 'to help maintain income in line with inflation.' The multiple mechanisms indicate the identified savings proposals do not alone close the deficit.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of the full gap-closure strategy; a finance director may be considering similar efficiency and income measures
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Alongside the proposals included in this consultation, we are already looking at other changes to save money or to be more efficient. This includes sharing senior managers with neighbouring councils, applying tighter controls before filling empty jobs, and reviewing internal processes to identify savings.

findings.headline: Specified savings total £288,000 (commercial waste £75k, community grants £113k, sustainability £100k) with three proposals unquantified
findings.detail: Six proposals are consulted on. Three carry specified savings: stopping commercial waste collections (£75,000 per annum), reducing community grant allocations and withdrawing capital grants (£113,000 total), and cutting the sustainability budget by one-third to £200,000 (£100,000 saving). Three further proposals — Grounds Maintenance Review, Information Offices hours, and Public Toilets closures/transfers — are marked 'tbc' with no figures. The paper explicitly states these proposals are 'not the only actions the council is taking to address its budget gap.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the full savings plan; consultation proposals alone appear to cover only 23% of the 2027/28 deficit, suggesting reliance on other undisclosed measures
findings.figures: £75,000, £113,000, £100,000; three items marked 'tbc'
findings.quote: The proposals below are not the only actions the council is taking to address its budget gap. They are included because they may have a more direct impact on services used by residents, businesses and community organisations.

findings.headline: New Forest forecasts budget gaps of £1.250 million in 2027/28 and £2.443 million in 2028/29, primarily from changes in Government funding
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Plan forecasts deficits of £1.25 million in 2027/28 rising to £2.44 million in 2028/29, attributed mainly to reduced central government funding. This represents a material challenge for a council with a discretionary services budget of approximately £59 million across waste, housing, environment, planning and regulatory functions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council can credibly close a material deficit; a finance director needs to understand how peer authorities are managing government funding reductions
findings.quote: The Council, as detailed in its Medium Term Financial Plan report to Cabinet in October 2026, is forecasting a budget gap of £1.250 million in 2027/28, increasing to £2.443 million in 2028/29. This is mainly due to changes in Government funding for local councils

findings.headline: HRA holds £9.7m in reserves (working balance, capital receipts, development reserves) available for budget gaps but explicitly flagged as one-time only resources
findings.detail: The council holds an HRA working balance of £1m, Capital Receipts Reserve of £3.942m, and Acquisitions and Development Reserve of £4.776m, totalling £9.718m. The paper notes that reserves "can only be used once and would reduce the resources available to fund future years' capital programmes," cautioning against relying on them as a solution to the emerging deficit. This signals reserves are being preserved for capital funding rather than operational deficits.
findings.matters: Reserves are a finite contingency against budget pressures. The explicit warning that they are one-time resources shows the council recognises they cannot be the answer to structural deficit. The size of reserves relative to the forecast deficit suggests some headroom, but only for a limited period.
findings.figures: HRA working balance £1m; Capital Receipts Reserve £3.942m; Acquisitions and Development Reserve £4.776m; total £9.718m
findings.quote: Reserves could be used to fund expenditure budget gaps, but only as a short-term measure. They can only be used once and would reduce the resources available to fund future years' capital programmes.

findings.headline: Council reviewing discretionary principal debt repayment of £3.769m in 2026/27 as potential lever to support medium-term budget balance
findings.detail: The HRA currently makes voluntary annual principal repayments of £3.769m in 2026/27 (historical level approximately £4.1m). These are discretionary, not statutory requirements. The paper signals that the council is considering varying this repayment level "to support the medium-term financial position, subject to maintaining the long-term sustainability of the HRA." This is framed as an option to address the emerging deficit forecast while preserving long-term resilience—a trade-off between near-term budget flexibility and future borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Discretionary debt management decisions affect both short-term budget balance and long-term financial resilience. Reducing debt repayment improves near-term cash position but increases future interest costs. This signals the council is weighing options; the choice made will indicate financial strategy direction.
findings.figures: Current repayment £3.769m (2026/27); historical level approximately £4.1m
findings.quote: As these repayments are discretionary rather than statutory, consideration could be given to varying the level of repayment to support the medium-term financial position, subject to maintaining the long-term sustainability of the HRA.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme includes £15.2m annual housing delivery funding and £15m by 2030 for decarbonisation, with estimated financing costs based on averages and flagged as subject to material variation
findings.detail: The council plans £15.2m per annum for new affordable housing (funded from capital receipts and new borrowing) and £3m in 2027/28 rising to £15m by 2030 for greener housing upgrades to meet EPC C by 2030, with a further £115m required by 2050 for net zero. The paper explicitly states that estimated financing costs (interest and principal repayments) are "based on averages and could vary materially, depending on development timetables." Detailed projects are not yet known, creating forecast uncertainty on both spending and financing assumptions.
findings.matters: Capital programme scale and financing assumptions are material to medium-term budget forecasts. Acknowledged uncertainty on timing and costs is a risk flag: the £15.2m annual housing programme plus £3m-£15m decarbonisation spending could shift materially, changing both capital receipts requirements and debt service costs.
findings.figures: Housing delivery £15.2m per annum; decarbonisation £3m (2027/28), £15m by 2030, £115m by 2050; financing costs estimated but acknowledged as subject to material variation
findings.quote: estimated financing costs (interest and loan principal repayments) are based on averages and could vary materially, depending on development timetables.

findings.headline: HRA plan assumes rent convergence policy with £1-£2 per week additional charge above CPI+1% from April 2027, closing gap created by 2023/24 rent restriction
findings.detail: Government guidelines allow CPI+1% rent increases to 2035/36 (assumed 3.9% in 2027/28, 3% thereafter). The council additionally assumes rent convergence: an extra £1 per week in 2027/28, then £2 per week from 2028 above CPI+1%, to close the gap between actual and formula rents. This gap opened when government capped 2023/24 increases at 7% instead of 11.1%. The convergence policy is material to the forecast income position but was delayed from April 2026 to April 2027 and requires Cabinet approval in February 2027. Context: 66% of tenants receive Housing Benefits or Universal Credit.
findings.matters: Rent income is the HRA's primary revenue source. Policy changes to allowable increases directly affect forecast balance. Convergence policy has not yet been legislated and is assumed but not confirmed. Tenant benefit-dependency (66%) creates affordability and collection risk that affects income reliability.
findings.figures: CPI 2.9% (July 2026); assumed rent increases 3.9% (2027/28), 3% per annum thereafter; convergence premium £1 per week (2027/28), £2 per week (2028 onwards); 66% of tenants on state support
findings.quote: 2027/28 weekly rents will be permitted to rise by £1 over and above CPI+1% and then by £2 above CPI+1% from 2028, until formula rent levels are reached.

findings.headline: Awaab's Law compliance, equal pay tribunal claims, and LGR transition costs create material unquantified budget pressures shown as open items in 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The council identifies three unresolved financial pressures with no figures yet attached: implementation of Awaab's Law (housing safety legislation putting "significant extra pressures on budgets and staffing" under current review); equal pay claims related to historic working practices proceeding to tribunal (financial impact unknown, council has not accepted claims); and ongoing Local Government Reorganisation transition costs (amount being quantified). The MTFP appendix shows these as "?" in the budget requirement sections, indicating they remain to be resolved before February 2027.
findings.matters: Finance directors manage contingencies and hidden liabilities. Unquantified pressures create budget planning uncertainty. Equal pay tribunal outcomes, regulatory compliance costs, and LGR transitions can each represent material budget demands that are not yet incorporated into the forecast position.
findings.figures: Impact not yet quantified, shown as "?" in budget requirement lines for 2027/28 and onwards
findings.quote: Commitments arising from changing legislation, particularly Awaab's Law, are putting significant extra pressures on budgets and staffing. A review of required resources is currently being carried out and is expected to result in a recommendation for additional budget provision.

findings.headline: Interest rates at circa 5% compared to 13-year average below 0.5%, with HRA financing costs rising to £870,000 in 2028/29
findings.detail: The council notes that base rates have risen from a 13-year average of less than 0.5% to approximately 5%. HRA financing costs (interest on borrowing) are forecast to rise from £550,000 in 2027/28 to £870,000 in 2028/29. This tenfold increase in funding cost reflects both the rate environment and the scale of the capital programme (housing delivery at £15.2m annually plus decarbonisation investment). The paper describes this as a significant external pressure on the HRA.
findings.matters: Lenders assess councils' exposure to rate movements and refinancing risk. A council with substantial borrowing sees material budget impact from sustained higher rates. The scale of increase (13-year average to 5%) is material context for financial sustainability and constrains other policy choices.
findings.figures: Base rate 5.25% peak (2023/24), currently 3.75%; 13-year average less than 0.5%; current region 5%; financing costs 2027/28 £550,000, 2028/29 £870,000
findings.quote: interest rate that has steeply risen from a 13-year average of less than 0.5% to a new level in the region of 5%

findings.headline: HRA forecast to move from surplus in 2027/28 to deficit of £190,000 by 2030/31
findings.detail: The council forecasts a surplus of £406,000 in 2027/28, declining through £310,000 (2028/29) and £40,000 (2029/30) to a deficit of £190,000 by 2030/31. This trajectory reflects the accumulated impact of pay and price inflation against income growth, even assuming rent convergence is implemented. The shift from sustained surplus to deficit signals a structural balance issue emerging over the medium term.
findings.matters: Finance directors track medium-term solvency; lenders require evidence of financial sustainability. A council moving into deficit by year four requires either savings, income growth, or reserve drawdown to remain balanced, and a small deficit is a flag for what follows.
findings.quote: Whilst the HRA is forecast to remain in surplus in the short term, this position reduces over time, resulting in a forecast deficit of £190,000 in 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report (based on performance April to June 2026 inclusive)
findings.headline: Milford-on-Sea Seafront Regeneration Scheme redesignated to longer-term, leaving £50,000 expenditure to be funded by council
findings.detail: The Milford-on-Sea Seafront Regeneration Scheme has been redesignated from immediate delivery to a longer-term proposal for consideration by the future Mid-Hampshire Unitary Authority. This means development work already undertaken will be sunk cost and the council will likely need to fund £50,000 of expenditure incurred to date from its own resources rather than recovering it from the scheme.
findings.matters: Scheme abandonment wastes development costs and capital funding. The redesignation signals the council's capital plans are being disrupted by local government reorganization uncertainty.
findings.figures: £50,000 of expenditure incurred to date on Milford scheme
findings.quote: Cabinet agreed to redesignate the Milford-on-Sea Seafront Regeneration Scheme from an immediate delivery project to a longer-term proposal for consideration by the future Mid-Hampshire Unitary Authority. As a result, it is likely that NFDC will need to fund expenditure incurred to date of £50,000 from its own resources.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report (based on performance April to June 2026 inclusive)
findings.headline: Planning appeal costs £130,000 with explicit warning of further expenditure risk
findings.detail: Three significant planning cases are currently under appeal. Costs to date are primarily legal advice, specialist consultant input, appeal preparation and attendance. The document explicitly flags that there is a risk further costs will be incurred.
findings.matters: Appeal costs are inherently unpredictable and can escalate substantially. Multiple concurrent cases magnify the risk of blowouts.
findings.figures: £130,000 to date on three cases
findings.quote: Development Management (£130,000) - Planning appeal costs continue to be incurred in relation to three significant cases currently under appeal. Expenditure to date principally relates to legal advice, specialist consultant input and appeal preparation plus attendance and there is a risk further costs will be incurred.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report (based on performance April to June 2026 inclusive)
findings.headline: Pay award negotiations unresolved with union claim for £3,000 or 10% whichever greater, employer offer 3.3% against 3.2% council assumption
findings.detail: The 2026/27 Local Government Services pay award remains unresolved. Union claim is for £3,000 or 10% (whichever greater) with industrial action processes underway. Employer offer of 3.3% exceeds the council's 3.2% assumption by 0.1%, which the council says contingency can cover—but only if the settlement does not worsen.
findings.matters: If pay negotiations settle higher than the 3.2% assumption, additional budget pressure will follow. Pay is typically the largest council budget item. Loss of contingency creates vulnerability to other unforeseen costs.
findings.figures: 3.3% employer offer vs 3.2% council assumption, 0.1% gap. Union claim: £3,000 or 10% whichever is greater.
findings.quote: There remains a financial risk that additional budget provision may be required, depending on the outcome of national negotiations and the final settlement and whether the remaining contingency budget can fund it.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report (based on performance April to June 2026 inclusive)
findings.headline: Investment property income £80,000 lower than forecast due to vacancies
findings.detail: Commercial investment property income is underperforming forecast by £70,000, with an additional £10,000 in unexpected business rates charges for void periods. This signals asset portfolio underutilization.
findings.matters: Commercial property income is often a core funding source for councils. A £80,000 shortfall indicates the portfolio is not performing as expected and may signal broader property market challenges.
findings.figures: £70,000 income shortfall plus £10,000 additional business rates for void periods = £80,000 total adverse variance
findings.quote: Investment Properties (£80,000) – Income is currently anticipated to be £70,000 less than estimate and additional business rates costs of £10,000 are to be incurred for void periods.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report (based on performance April to June 2026 inclusive)
findings.headline: £161,000 supplementary budget required for mandatory electrical compliance works at residential park site
findings.detail: Stillwater Park is a 69-plot residential park home site owned and operated by the council. An electrical infrastructure assessment identified aging equipment requiring replacement and standardization of legacy connection methods to meet current standards. The council has statutory duties as site operator to maintain electrical infrastructure in a safe and compliant condition.
findings.matters: This is an unbudgeted mandatory compliance cost that cannot be deferred. Electrical safety failures could expose the council to legal and safety liability.
findings.figures: £161,000 total, 69 plots, approximately £2,330 per plot
findings.quote: an estimated cost of c£2,330 per plot has been established. Applying this across 69 plots gives a baseline estimated programme cost of £161,000

findings.headline: Housing maintenance complaints rose to 76 from 45 in 2025/26, with compensation payments totalling £21,581
findings.detail: Housing maintenance complaints reached 76 in 2025/26, up from 45 the prior year. Compensation payments totalled £21,581. The council is developing a formal compensation policy to standardise these payments. Recurring themes include delays, cancellations with poor communication, and quality of repairs.
findings.matters: Rising compensation and complaint volumes signal service deterioration and unbudgeted costs; the need for a compensation policy suggests the council recognises liability exposure.
findings.figures: 76 complaints (vs 45); compensation payments £21,581
findings.quote: Compensation payments arising from complaints have increased, totalling £21,581 in the last financial year. The Council is currently developing a compensation policy to standardise payments and ensure a fair and consistent approach where services have not met agreed standards.

findings.headline: Housing capital programme of £31,550 million proposed for 2026/27, including fire remediation
findings.detail: The council proposes housing capital expenditure of £31,550 million for 2026/27. Major commitments include £1.3 million for fire remediation works (with £850,000 rephased from 2025/26), £10.7 million for major repairs, and £3 million for home energy improvements. Fire remediation covers two schemes (Whitecroft in Hythe and Clarks Close in Ringwood) requiring fire safety strategy updates.
findings.matters: A lender needs clarity on how this significant capital commitment is funded and how it affects debt service or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £31,550 million total; £1.3 million fire remediation; £10.7 million major repairs; £3 million home energy
findings.quote: The proposed Housing Public Sector capital expenditure programme for 2026/27 totals £31550 million. Significant works to properties, including mandatory compartmentation and new fire doors, are being carried out following detailed Fire Risk Assessment surveys. Funding of £1.3 million is proposed for 2026/27, including £850,000 rephased from 2025/26. The Major Repairs budget has been set at £10.7 million.

findings.headline: 49% of domestic housing stock remains without asbestos survey coverage
findings.detail: Asbestos survey information exists for only 51% of the council's domestic housing stock. The report cites budget and contractor capacity constraints as limiting factors. The annual asbestos budget is £100,000, of which 60% is allocated to removal, leaving £40,000 for surveys and testing. A targeted improvement programme is promised once capacity increases, but no timeline is provided.
findings.matters: Unsurveyed council housing is a latent compliance and liability risk; the council has identified it but not resourced it adequately.
findings.figures: 51% of domestic stock surveyed; £40,000 annual budget available for surveys; £100,000 total annual asbestos budget
findings.quote: Currently, asbestos survey information is held for approximately 51% of the Council's domestic housing stock. Progress in this area is constrained by available contractor capacity, and the need to gain access to tenants' homes. The current annual domestic asbestos budget is £100,000, of which approximately 60% is allocated to removal works. This leaves around £40,000 available to support additional survey and testing activity.

findings.headline: Repairs service demand rising 9% with insufficient budget identified
findings.detail: The Repairs Service received 23,030 repairs in 2025/26, up 1,933 from the previous year. Complaints rose from 45 to 76. The council explicitly stated to EMT on 28 April that the service faces pressure, and the report notes: Additional resources are now required to support legislative change and rising demand. A wider review of resource requirements is underway but no funding decision is documented.
findings.matters: A council admitting it needs additional resources for a core service, without documented funding, signals either budget pressure or unmet liabilities.
findings.figures: 23,030 repairs (9.16% increase); 76 complaints vs 45 prior year; emergency repairs compliance at 84.22% against 90% target
findings.quote: Additional resources are now required to support legislative change and rising demand, to ensure strong Tenant Satisfaction Measure performance can be maintained and best-practice service delivery continues.

findings.headline: Recycling income shortfalls across glass (£47k), textiles (£35k), and trade waste (£19k)
findings.detail: The refuse and recycling service saw income fall short in three separate waste streams, totalling £101k revenue loss, suggesting structural market pressures on secondary materials rather than operational issues.
findings.matters: Multiple shortfalls across waste streams indicate market-wide pressures on recyclables income that may be structural and persistent, reducing revenue reliability.
findings.figures: Glass £47,000; Textiles £35,000; Trade Waste £19,000; total £101,000
findings.quote: income receipts were lower than budgeted for Glass (£47,000), Textiles (£35,000) and Trade Waste (£19,000) services.

findings.headline: Capital programme rephasing: £1.561 million deferred to future years

findings.headline: Council creating £500,000 reserve to fund retention of business-critical staff due to Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The council has adopted a Market Supplement Policy in response to LGR and is establishing a new £500k Staff Retention Reserve, intended to fund retention arrangements for business-critical roles through 2026/27 and 2027/28.

findings.matters: This indicates a significant structural budget gap ahead that the council has not yet solved. Lenders need confidence in how a £1.5m shortfall will be closed.

findings.paper_title: Report - SAMP Strategic Asset Management Plan Progress Report - July 2026 Cabinet Final (3)
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation splits New Forest district between two unitary authorities, creating asset apportionment and transition risk
findings.detail: Government decision to proceed with LGR in Hampshire will divide New Forest between two new councils. The Waterside parishes (Fawley, Hythe and Dibden, Marchwood, Totton and Eling) transfer to a Southampton/Eastleigh unitary authority, while the majority joins a Test Valley/Winchester/East Hampshire authority. The council is establishing a Property and Estates LGR workstream to manage controlled transfer of 366 assets valued at £107m to successor authorities.
findings.matters: Fundamental structural change affecting council viability, service continuity, and asset management post-transfer; creates operational risks during transition and requires evidence-led decision-making on asset apportionment to withstand future scrutiny.
findings.figures: 366 non-housing assets valued at over £107 million spanning approximately 770 hectares; four Waterside parishes affected by boundary change
findings.quote: Because the current district is being divided, there is a clear requirement to understand how assets, services and staff will be apportioned between the two future authorities.

findings.paper_title: Report - SAMP Strategic Asset Management Plan Progress Report - July 2026 Cabinet Final (3)
findings.headline: £2m Public Conveniences capital replacement programme commits to demolition and new build at three priority sites
findings.detail: New Forest has identified three public convenience locations for demolition and replacement with standardised modular units: New Street Lymington, Calshot Beach East, and Betsy Lane Bransgore. A fourth site (Library Road Totton) has been deferred due to uncertainty around the Totton Masterplan. The programme uses condition surveys and usage data to prioritise investment, employing a managed Design and Build procurement route.
findings.matters: Material capital expenditure with defined scope and tight timescale driven by Local Government Reorganisation deadline; procurement strategy and site selection reflect shifting from site-by-site reactive decisions to strategic portfolio management.
findings.figures: £2m allocated capital sum for multi-year project; 23 public convenience blocks assessed; three priority replacement sites
findings.quote: As part of the portfolio-wide review, four Public Convenience blocks were initially identified where refurbishment would not deliver a sustainable or compliant outcome and where demolition and replacement provide the most appropriate solution. These sites have been prioritised based on a combination of poor building condition, functional obsolescence, accessibility constraints and whole-life cost considerations.

findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's independent decision-making window is closing; future budgets will be determined by a restructured authority with different governance and accountability.

findings.detail: The alternative budget redirects £770k from the Corporate Priorities reserve to fund policy initiatives, with the originally planned Public Conveniences refurbishment deferred and reclassified as capital spending instead. This shows a strategic shift in how reserves are committed.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion patterns and changes in planned use indicate the council's financial flexibility and liquidity position during a period of governance transition.

findings.detail: Liberal Democrats propose borrowing £1m for a Warm Spaces Grant Programme to create community spaces as warm hubs. They argue this is modest borrowing against the council's existing £132.9m debt and claim it will not 'realistically affect the overall financial situation'.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's debt capacity needs to see all proposed new borrowing and the council's assessment of its proportionate impact on an already substantial debt base.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - AMR Programme and GF Capital Programme Report
findings.headline: Council is committing to £2.947m borrowing for vehicles and plant replacement in 2026/27, with multi-year programme totalling £7.4m
findings.detail: The general fund capital programme includes £2.947m of external borrowing for vehicle and plant replacement in 2026/27, with further commitments of £1.012m in 2027/28 and £3.458m in 2028/29. Depreciation charges on the vehicles are recorded in revenue and contribute to repayment through Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP). The council also has a separate £610k investment in waste collection vehicles following waste service implementation.
findings.matters: This represents a specific, quantified borrowing commitment that increases the council's debt service costs over multiple years. A lender would need to assess the adequacy of depreciation/MRP repayment rates and whether the council can absorb these costs alongside other spending pressures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - AMR Programme and GF Capital Programme Report
findings.headline: Marsh Lane Depot electrical infrastructure operating at full capacity with safety and compliance risks
findings.detail: Consultant feasibility work completed in 2025 found that the existing electrical infrastructure at Marsh Lane Depot (the council's main service depot) is operating at full capacity and poses compliance and safety risks. The council plans to invest £500k in 2026/27 to install a new 1500kVA substation. The upgrade is described as critical to provide capacity relief, improve resilience, and ensure statutory compliance while supporting future operational growth.
findings.matters: This is critical infrastructure at a key operational facility. Operating at full capacity with safety risks creates vulnerability to service interruption. Failure could impact the council's ability to deliver waste, environmental and fleet management services.
findings.figures: £500,000 capital investment in 2026/27; existing infrastructure at full capacity
findings.quote: the existing electrical infrastructure is operating at full capacity and poses compliance and safety risks. The upgrade will provide essential capacity relief, improve resilience, and ensure statutory compliance, while supporting future operational growth

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - AMR Programme and GF Capital Programme Report
findings.headline: Public Conveniences assessed as critical condition across four sites, requiring £2m refurbishment programme
findings.detail: Condition surveys undertaken in 2025 revealed significant structural and operational issues across the council's 23 public convenience sites. Four priority locations—Calshot East, Totton Central, Bransgore, and Lymington New Street—are in critical condition and require full refurbishment. The £2m investment is phased over 2026/27 and 2027/28, with works including health and safety compliance, accessibility improvements, and sustainability enhancements.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand why these assets deteriorated to critical condition, what this reveals about the council's asset management capability, and whether similar deterioration is occurring in other parts of the estate.

findings.headline: Debt service costs of £5.7m budgeted for 2026/27 on average portfolio of £150.8m at 3.77%, rising with forecast additional borrowing
findings.detail: The Council's budgeted debt interest for 2026/27 is £5.7m, based on an average debt portfolio of £150.8m at an average interest rate of 3.77%. As the Council takes on additional external borrowing to fund its growing capital programme, debt service costs will rise. Investment income is budgeted at £1.7m, giving a net treasury cost position of approximately £4m annually.
findings.matters: Rising debt service represents a growing, fixed claim on the revenue budget that must be funded from council tax, business rates and government grants. As borrowing increases, this becomes an increasingly significant revenue pressure.
findings.figures: Debt interest budget 2026/27: £5.7m. Average debt portfolio: £150.8m. Average interest rate: 3.77%. Investment income budget: £1.7m.
findings.quote: the budget for debt interest paid in 2026/27 is £5.7m, based on an average debt portfolio of £150.8m at an average interest rate of 3.77%.

findings.headline: New commercial and residential investment schemes suspended due to current interest rates making them unviable
findings.detail: The Council has put on hold new investment in commercial and residential property schemes that it had previously been pursuing. The reason given is that current interest rate levels make the economic case for these schemes marginal or negative. This represents a strategic retreat from income-generating investment activity.
findings.matters: The suspension signals the Council is constrained in its ability to generate new rental income streams at current borrowing costs. For a council facing reserve depletion and growing capital commitments, loss of this diversification opportunity weakens its financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Investment schemes suspended; no new loan book impact in current forecast period.
findings.quote: New commercial and residential investment schemes have currently been put on hold due to the current interest rates making schemes less viable.

findings.headline: Pooled fund investments carrying £0.336m unrealised loss, with mandatory statutory override expiry on 31 March 2028
findings.detail: The Council's pooled fund investments (property and equity) are currently valued at a loss of £0.336m against cost. A statutory override under IFRS 9 exempts local authorities from recognising these losses in the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement, but this exemption expires 31 March 2028 for pre-April 2024 investments. The Council has established a Treasury Management Reserve of £0.300m to mitigate risk, but this is insufficient to cover the full current loss.
findings.matters: The override expiry creates a known future impact on the Council's accounts. If markets do not recover or decline further by 2028, this loss will reduce reported net worth and could consume the Treasury Management Reserve, weakening the Council's reported financial position.
findings.figures: Unrealised loss: £0.336m. Treasury Management Reserve: £0.300m. Statutory override expires 31 March 2028.
findings.quote: At the current time, the Council's pooled fund investments are valued with an unrealised capital loss of £0.336m. To date, the statutory override in place of IFRS 9 for local authorities exempts the Council from taking this unrealised loss to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement (CIES). This override has been extended to 31 March 2028 for investments made before 1 April 2024, at which time the Council will be expected to reflect any gains and losses in the CIES.

findings.headline: Balance sheet resources depleting from £53.8m to £35.6m (34% decline), forcing shift from internal to external borrowing
findings.detail: The Council's usable reserves are forecast to decline significantly over the period, from £53.8m in 2026 to £35.6m by 2029. Meanwhile, internal borrowing (using reserves to avoid external debt) is rising to £121.7m by 2029. The liability benchmark analysis confirms the Council will need to access external borrowing to fund the gap between its CFR and available resources.
findings.matters: A 34% depletion of reserves over three years materially reduces the Council's financial flexibility and cushion for unexpected costs. The transition to external borrowing signals the Council's underlying capital commitments outpace its revenue generation.
findings.figures: Balance sheet resources: £53.8m (2026 estimate) declining to £35.6m (2029). Internal borrowing forecast to reach £121.7m by 2029 vs £65.3m in 2026.
findings.quote: The Council expects a positive liability benchmark across the forecast period, due to a rising CFR in combination with an expectation that balance sheet resources will drop, which generally means an authority is required to take external borrowing to fund the gap between its resources and the CFR.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account capital financing requirement rising to £87.8m by 2028/29, driven by housing improvements and development
findings.detail: The HRA CFR is forecast to grow from £37.9m (31 March 2026 estimate) to £52.4m (2027), £69.6m (2028) and £87.8m (2029). This represents the dominant driver of the Council's total CFR growth over the period, outpacing general fund pressures. The increases are attributable to housing maintenance, energy improvements and the development programme.
findings.matters: The HRA is normally a council's strongest revenue stream, but this trajectory shows major capital commitments ahead, which will require either revenue surpluses or additional borrowing to service. It signals a significant shift in the council's capital intensity.
findings.figures: HRA CFR: £37.9m (2026 estimate), £52.4m (2027), £69.6m (2028), £87.8m (2029). Total CFR grows from £178.2m to £214.9m over the same period.
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) CFR is also increasing as the Council looks to deliver the requirements arising from Housing Energy Improvements, Planned Maintenance and the current Housing Development Programme.

findings.headline: Long-term affordability explicitly depends on service savings being delivered and continued government transitional support
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer states that medium-to-long-term affordability of the capital programme is contingent on two conditions: (1) service change savings must be delivered as planned, and (2) government must continue transitional support for the waste strategy rollout and HRA decarbonisation. If either condition is not met, the programme becomes unaffordable.
findings.matters: This is a frank acknowledgement of affordability risk. It signals that the council cannot sustain the capital programme from core revenue without relying on external conditions (government support and internal transformation).
findings.figures: Capital programme over 2026-2029: £142.414m total; HRA decarbonisation is flagged as a major cost driver requiring support
findings.quote: the medium-long term affordability remains reliant on service change savings being delivered, and government transitional support (with regards to the waste strategy roll-out & the large decarbonisation requirements within the HRA).

findings.headline: Commercial property investment strategy paused because interest costs exceed expected returns
findings.detail: The council previously approved strategies for commercial (£50m limit) and residential (£10m limit) property investment for economic sustainability and income generation. New expenditure under these strategies remains paused because the council is now in an external borrowing position, and the cost of that debt exceeds the income yields available on investment properties.
findings.matters: A paused investment strategy signals that the council has revised its risk appetite downward due to financing costs, and that investment-driven income cannot offset borrowing costs.
findings.figures: Commercial investment property valued at £28.3m; approved limits £50m commercial, £10m residential
findings.quote: Expenditure on these approved strategies remains paused due to the interest return that can currently be received on cash balances, and as the Council is now in an external borrowing position, the interest charges are currently too high to satisfy the financial parameters of the business case requirements.

findings.headline: Cash reserves being drawn down to a £10m minimum to fund the capital programme through internal borrowing
findings.detail: The council holds £32.4m of investments as at March 2025, but plans to reduce near-term investments from £23.3m to £10m and hold it there. This £10m is identified as the absolute minimum working balance. The drawn-down cash is used as internal borrowing to fund capital spend before external loans become necessary.
findings.matters: Declining liquidity reduces the council's buffer against revenue shortfalls or unexpected costs and increases reliance on debt markets during adverse conditions.
findings.figures: Table 8: Near-term investments 2025 actual £23.3m, 2026 forecast £10.0m, 2027-2029 budgets £10m-£10.3m
findings.quote: the majority of the Council's cash will be utilised over the period through internal borrowing to fund the needs of the Council's capital programme, until minimum balances reach £10 million

findings.headline: Financing costs rising significantly as a proportion of revenue, particularly in HRA (reaching 20.4% by 2028)
findings.detail: Interest and MRP charges on debt are rising sharply. General Fund financing costs rise from 11.5% to 13.1% of net revenue stream; HRA financing costs rise from 15.2% to 20.4%. With HRA at 20.4%, nearly a fifth of HRA rental income is committed to debt servicing, constraining capacity for maintenance and new build.
findings.matters: Financing costs crowding out service delivery budgets is a key risk indicator for lenders; HRA at 20.4% leaves limited headroom for expense shocks.
findings.quote: The Financing costs of both the General Fund and HRA are set to increase as a result of the required Capital Financing Requirement, reducing cash balances (and assumed interest rates) for investment and costs of external borrowing

findings.headline: Total outstanding debt projected to rise from £141.3m to £197.6m over four years, with capital programme debt nearly trebling
findings.detail: The council's total debt is forecast to grow substantially. More significantly, the debt specifically attributable to the capital programme (not the HRA settlement debt from 2012) is expected to grow from £35.5m to £104.1m between 2026 and 2029. This tripling of capital-related debt over four years is a major structural change.
findings.matters: Rapidly growing debt levels increase refinancing risk and constrain financial capacity, particularly important given the shift to external borrowing in a higher interest rate environment.
findings.figures: Table 6: Total debt 2026 forecast £141.3m, 2029 budget £197.6m; Debt–Capital programme 2026 forecast £35.5m, 2029 budget £104.1m
